entities.name: The City of God
entities.label: Text
entities.summary: The City of God is a literary work from the Classical era, born out of the Roman Empire's transformation into a Christian entity. It was written by St. Augustine of Hippo in 419 CE, in response to the sacking of Rome by Alaric's Visigoths, and became a foundational text of Christian theology. The work frames the City of God as a spiritual realm that transcends the earthly city of Rome, influencing Western Christianity's understanding of salvation and the nature of God. This concept has continued to shape Western philosophy and politics, particularly in the context of the Crusades and the Reformation. The City of God's influence can be seen in the works of Thomas Aquinas and Martin Luther, who both referenced Augustine's ideas in their own theological and philosophical writings. The text's impact on the development of medieval thought and its ongoing relevance in contemporary debates about the nature of God and salvation make it a significant entity in the historical record. The City of God's legacy can be seen in the continued relevance of its ideas in modern Western culture, where the concept of the 'City of God' remains a powerful symbol of Christian values and ideals.
